name: Sterling Atlas 3/4 in Rigging Rope
title: Sterling Atlas 3/4 in Rigging Rope
meta: Sterling Atlas rigging rope in 3/4 in diameter for lowering big wood and heavy tops. What it suits, how to set it up, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A 3/4 in rigging line for crews lowering heavy wood on removals.
summary: Sterling Atlas rigging rope in 3/4 in is a heavy lowering line for removal crews that regularly block down big wood. The diameter gives you more strength and more to hold onto on the port-a-wrap than a 1/2 or 5/8 line.
highlights: Made for lowering lines and speed lines
Large diameter is easy on the hands at the friction device
Pairs with large blocks and heavy-duty slings
Sold by length in a hank

body.h: Where a 3/4 in line fits on the job
p: Most climbers rig small to mid-size pieces on 1/2 or 5/8 rope. A 3/4 in line like Sterling Atlas comes out when the wood gets heavy: big leaders on a removal, long spar sections blocked down with a large rigging block, or a crane-free takedown over a roof. The extra diameter adds strength and gives the groundie more rope to control the run.

The tradeoff is weight and bulk. A 3/4 in line fills a rope bag fast, needs a block and lowering device sized for it, and takes more effort to pull back up. Many crews keep one heavy line on the truck for the big jobs and run lighter rope day to day. See other options in rigging rope.

Match the rope to your block sheave, port-a-wrap or capstan, and slings so that every part of the system is sized for the loads you plan to put on it. Confirm the rated strength with the seller and leave a healthy margin for shock loading when you let pieces run.

Look for glazing, pulled strands, cuts, and stiff or flat sections after each job, and retire rope that has taken a hard shock load or shows core damage. Keep it out of bar oil and fuel and store it dry. Rig only within the rated strength of every component in the system, inspect the rope before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is 3/4 in rope overkill for most tree work?
faq.a: For pruning and small removals, usually yes. It earns its place when you are blocking down heavy wood and want more strength and control at the lowering device.

faq.q: Can I use a rigging rope for climbing?
faq.a: No. Rigging rope is for moving wood. Climb only on rope made and rated for life support.

name: Teufelberger Sirius Bull Rope 12mm
title: Teufelberger Sirius Bull Rope 12mm Rigging Line
meta: Teufelberger Sirius bull rope in 12mm, a lighter rigging line for pruning wood and small tops. What it handles, sizing, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A 12mm Teufelberger rigging line for lowering wood on pruning and removal jobs.
summary: The Teufelberger Sirius bull rope in 12mm is a rigging line built for lowering wood, not for climbing. At 12mm it is the lightest of the three and the easiest to handle for pruning-size wood, small tops, and tag lines.
highlights: Runs through blocks and friction devices
Part of the Teufelberger Sirius line
Available in several diameters to match the job

body.h: What the 12mm size is good for
p: A bull rope takes the load every time a piece is cut and caught, so the diameter you pick decides what you can safely lower. The 12mm Sirius bull rope is the lightest of the three and the easiest to handle for pruning-size wood, small tops, and tag lines. It runs through a rigging block, a port-a-wrap, or a capstan winch like any other rigging line.

Size matters at both ends of the rope. Thinner line is lighter to haul up and quicker to reset, while thicker line spreads the load over more fibers and gives the ground person more to grip. Compare sizes in rigging rope before you buy.

body.h: Matching it to your gear and keeping it in service
p: Check that your block sheave, lowering device, and slings accept the diameter and are rated for the loads you plan to put through them. Confirm the rope's rated strength with the seller, and remember that letting a piece run builds far more force than its static weight.

Inspect the full length after each job for cuts, glazing, pulled strands, and flat or stiff spots, and retire it after a severe shock load. Keep it clean and away from saw fuel and bar oil. Rig only within the rated strength of every component in the system, inspect the rope before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Which Sirius bull rope diameter should I buy?
faq.a: Pick by the wood you lower most often. 12mm suits pruning and small tops, 14mm covers most residential removals, and 16mm is for heavier blocking.

faq.q: Is a bull rope rated for climbing?
faq.a: No. A bull rope is for rigging only. Climb on rope made and rated for life support.

name: Yale Double Esterlon 3/4 in Rigging Rope
title: Yale Double Esterlon 3/4 in Rigging Rope
h1: Yale Double Esterlon 3/4 in Rigging Rope
meta: Yale Double Esterlon 3/4 in, a polyester double braid rigging rope for heavy lowering on removals. What it suits, sizing, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A 3/4 in polyester double braid rigging line from Yale Cordage.
summary: Yale Double Esterlon is a polyester double braid rigging rope, and the 3/4 in size is the heavy-duty size for big wood, large blocks, and long spar sections. Double braid construction makes it a good candidate for spliced eyes and a firm, round line through blocks.

p: Double Esterlon is a braid-on-braid polyester rope: a braided core inside a braided cover, with both sharing the load. Polyester stretches less than nylon, so pieces stop with less bounce, and the round, firm line feeds cleanly through a block and around a port-a-wrap. In 3/4 in it is the heavy-duty size for big wood, large blocks, and long spar sections.
Double braid also splices well, so many crews have an eye spliced into one end for a quick connection to a sling or carabiner. Browse other rigging rope if you need a lighter or heavier line.

Make sure the rope fits your block sheave and friction device and that every part of the system is rated for the loads you will generate. Confirm the rated strength with the seller, and allow for shock loading when pieces are let run.

After each job, run the rope through your hands looking for cuts, melted or glazed areas, cover damage that exposes the core, and lumps or flat spots. Retire it after a severe shock load. Rig only within the rated strength of every component in the system, inspect the rope before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is double braid better than 16-strand for rigging?
faq.a: Both work. Double braid is strong for its size and splices cleanly, while 16-strand is often easier to tie and grip. Many crews carry one of each.

faq.q: Is 3/4 in Double Esterlon too heavy for pruning?
faq.a: For light pruning, a 1/2 in line is easier to handle. The larger size pays off when the wood is heavy.

name: Yale Bee Line 10mm Polyester Core Hitch Cord
title: 10mm Polyester Core Bee Line Hitch Cord
h1: 10mm Polyester Core Bee Line Hitch Cord
meta: 10mm Bee Line hitch cord with a polyester core, sold by the foot for friction hitches and eye-to-eye prusiks. How to size it and when to retire it.
tagline: A 10mm hitch cord by the foot for climbers who tie their own friction hitches.
summary: This 10mm Bee Line hitch cord has a polyester core and is sold by the foot, so you can cut exactly what you need for a friction hitch or have eyes sewn or spliced. It suits climbers running thicker climbing lines who want a hitch that grips without locking up.
highlights: For Valdotain, Distel, and similar friction hitches
Thicker cord for larger climbing lines

p: Hitch cord diameter is about the pairing with your climbing line. A 10mm cord on a 11 to 13mm rope gives a hitch that grabs firmly but still slides when you tend it. On thinner climbing lines, a 10mm hitch can feel slow and you may prefer 8mm. Test any new pairing low to the ground before you trust it aloft.

Buying by the foot lets you cut a length for your preferred hitch and knot your own ends, or plan for sewn or spliced eyes. Compare other tech cordage and hitch cord if you are dialing in a combination.

Friction hitches build heat and wear quickly, and the hitch cord is usually the first part of a climbing system to wear out. Check it every day for glazing, fuzzing, stiffness, and cover wear, and replace it early rather than late. Burn-sealed cut ends should be finished cleanly so they do not catch.

The polyester core gives the cord a firm, round body that holds the shape of a hitch, and a 10mm cord has a little more material to spread heat on long descents. Climbers who move a lot of rope through a hitch on big trees often like that extra mass. It is also a forgiving size for learning to tie and dress a new hitch.
Hitch cord is life-support gear: use it only in a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every climb, and get trained before you tie into anything new.

faq.q: How much 10mm hitch cord do I need?
faq.a: It depends on the hitch and on knotted versus spliced ends. Many climbers buy enough for two cords so they always have a spare.

faq.q: Will 10mm cord work on an 11mm rope?
faq.a: It can, but the grip changes with each rope. Test the combination close to the ground and adjust the hitch before you climb on it.

name: Sterling 9mm Hitch Cord (By the Foot)
title: Sterling 9mm Hitch Cord by the Foot
h1: Sterling 9mm Hitch Cord, By the Foot
meta: Sterling 9mm hitch cord sold by the foot for friction hitches and eye-to-eye prusiks. Which climbing lines it pairs with and when to retire it.
tagline: A 9mm Sterling cord by the foot for building your own friction hitch.
summary: Sterling 9mm hitch cord sits between the common 8mm and 10mm sizes, giving climbers a middle option for friction hitches on popular arborist climbing lines. It is sold by the foot so you cut the length your hitch needs.
highlights: For friction hitches and eye-to-eye prusiks

p: A hitch that grabs too hard is tiring to tend; one that grabs too little is dangerous. Going from 8mm to 10mm changes the bite a lot, and a 9mm cord gives you a step in between. Climbers often reach for it when 8mm feels grabby on their line and 10mm feels slow.

Because you buy it by the foot, you can cut a length for a Valdotain, Distel, or other hitch, and finish the ends with knots or have eyes made. Look through other hitch cord and tech cordage to compare sizes.

Every hitch cord and climbing line combination behaves differently, and a new rope or a wet day can change it. Set up and test close to the ground before climbing, and adjust wraps and braids until the hitch holds and releases the way you want.

A by-the-foot cord also makes it easy to experiment. Cut one length for a Valdotain tresse and another for a Distel, climb on each for a week, and keep the one that suits your rope and style. Write down the length that works so you can cut replacements without guessing.

Check the cord daily for glazing, stiffness, and cover wear, and swap it out at the first sign of heat damage. Hitch cord is life-support gear: use it only in a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every climb, and get trained before you tie into anything new.

faq.q: Is 9mm hitch cord a good match for 11.7mm rope?
faq.a: Many climbers find the middle size works on common 11 to 12mm lines, but test your exact combination low before using it aloft.

faq.q: Can I tie my own eyes?
faq.a: You can finish the ends with appropriate stopper knots per training, or have eyes sewn or spliced by a qualified shop.

name: Teufelberger Sirius Reepschnur Accessory Cord (Per Foot)
title: Teufelberger Sirius Reepschnur Cord, Per Foot
meta: Teufelberger Sirius Reepschnur accessory cord sold by the foot for prusiks, tag lines, and gear tethers. What it is for and how to check it.
tagline: Teufelberger accessory cord by the foot for prusiks, tethers, and utility jobs.
summary: Teufelberger Reepschnur is accessory cord from the Sirius line, sold by the foot so you can cut prusik loops, tethers, and utility lengths. Reepschnur is simply the German word for accessory cord.
highlights: Cut to length for prusiks and tethers
Handy for tag lines and gear lanyards

body.h: What accessory cord does on a tree crew
p: Every climber ends up needing short lengths of good cord: a prusik to back up a rigging line, a tether for a hand saw, a loop to hang a water bottle, or a short tag line. Buying Reepschnur by the foot lets you cut what you need instead of buying pre-made pieces for each job.
Confirm the diameter you are ordering, since accessory cord is offered in several sizes and the right one depends on what you are tying it to. Browse other tech cordage for dedicated hitch cords.

Not every cord is meant for life support. Before you use any cord in a climbing system, confirm with the seller and the manufacturer's information that it is rated and intended for that use. For anything that holds a person, use a dedicated arborist hitch cord or a certified prusik.

Keeping a short hank of accessory cord in the gear bag saves a lot of improvising on the job. It ties off a loose limb before a cut, hangs a water jug in the shade, or rigs a quick tether for a pole saw head. Because you cut your own lengths, there is no waste and no hunting for the right pre-made loop.
Seal cut ends cleanly, check cord for abrasion and stiffness, and replace it once it is worn or has been heated. Train on any hitch you plan to use before you rely on it.

faq.q: What does Reepschnur mean?
faq.a: It is German for accessory cord, the small-diameter cord used for prusiks, tethers, and utility jobs.

faq.q: Can I use it as my climbing hitch cord?
faq.a: Only if the manufacturer rates that diameter for life-support friction hitches. Otherwise use a dedicated arborist hitch cord.

name: Yale Bee Line 8mm Hitch Cord (By the Foot)
title: Yale Bee Line 8mm Hitch Cord by the Foot
h1: Yale Bee Line 8mm Hitch Cord, By the Foot
meta: Yale Bee Line 8mm hitch cord, sold by the foot for friction hitches on arborist climbing lines. How to pair it with your rope and when to replace it.
tagline: Yale's 8mm Bee Line hitch cord, cut to length for your friction hitch.
summary: Yale Bee Line 8mm hitch cord is a popular choice for friction hitches on common 11 to 13mm arborist climbing lines. It is sold by the foot, so you can cut a length for your hitch of choice and keep a spare in the bag.
highlights: Common pairing for 11 to 13mm climbing lines
For Valdotain, Distel, and similar hitches

p: An 8mm hitch cord bites harder than a 10mm one on the same climbing line, which many climbers like on slick or larger-diameter rope. Bee Line has been a common pick for friction hitches for years, and buying it by the foot means you cut exactly the length your hitch and knot style need.

Pair it with your rope, then test the hitch low before climbing: wraps, braids, and the rope's condition all change how it grips and releases. See more hitch cord and tech cordage if you want to compare diameters.

The hitch cord takes the heat on every descent, so it wears long before your climbing line. Look for glazing, a hard or flattened feel, cover fuzz, and any spot that feels different from the rest. Swap it out early; it is the cheapest part of your system.

Buying by the foot also means you can keep a spare length rolled in your bag. When a hitch starts to glaze mid-job, you can cut and tie a fresh one at the base of the tree instead of calling it a day. Cut a little long at first, then trim once you know the length your hitch needs.
Hitch cord is life-support gear: use it only in a system that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, inspect it before every climb, and get trained before you tie into anything new.

faq.q: Should I buy 8mm or 10mm Bee Line?
faq.a: 8mm grips harder on the same line; 10mm runs smoother. Pick based on your climbing rope and test both if you can.

faq.q: How long should a hitch cord be?
faq.a: It depends on the hitch and how the ends are finished. Measure an existing cord you like, or buy extra and trim after testing.

name: Yale Ultrex 5/16 in Winch Line with Chook
title: Yale Ultrex 5/16 in Winch Line with Chook
h1: Yale Ultrex 5/16 in Winch Line with Chook
meta: Yale Ultrex 5/16 in synthetic winch line with a Chook hook end. Why crews swap steel cable for synthetic, how to fit it, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A 5/16 in Ultrex synthetic winch line with a Chook end, ready to spool.
summary: Yale Ultrex winch line in 5/16 in, supplied with a Chook end fitting, is a synthetic replacement for steel winch cable that is ready to put on the drum. Synthetic line is light, floats, and does not kink or leave broken wire strands to catch your hands.
highlights: Supplied with a Chook end fitting
Lighter and easier to handle than steel cable
No broken wire strands to snag gloves
For winches on trucks, chippers, and skid steers

body.h: Why switch from steel to synthetic
p: Steel winch cable is heavy, kinks, and frays into sharp wire ends that cut through gloves. A synthetic winch line like Ultrex is a fraction of the weight, flexes easily around the drum, and is far nicer to drag out to a log or a stuck truck. Crews use it on truck and chipper winches, skid steers, and log arches.

This 5/16 in version comes with a Chook end, so it is ready to attach to the drum and go to work. Check that the size matches your winch's specification and fairlead. Other rigging rope and winch line options are in the same category.

Synthetic line works best with a smooth hawse fairlead rather than worn rollers that can pinch it. Spool it on under some tension so the wraps do not bury themselves under load, and keep it away from hot exhaust and sharp edges.

A lighter line also helps the groundie. Pulling out to a log or a hung-up top over rough ground is much easier with synthetic, and it does not spring back with stored energy the way a kinked steel cable can. It also coils neatly on the truck without leaving sharp burrs in your gloves.

Inspect synthetic winch line for cuts, abrasion, melted or fused fibers, and heavy discoloration, and replace it if the line is damaged. Keep everyone out of the line of pull while winching, and use the winch and line only within their rated capacity and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Can I put synthetic line on a winch built for steel cable?
faq.a: Often yes, but check the winch maker's guidance, replace worn roller fairleads or switch to a hawse fairlead, and confirm the line's rating matches the winch.

faq.q: What is the Chook?
faq.a: It is the end fitting supplied on this line from Yale Cordage. Confirm its rating with the seller and use it within that limit.

name: Yale Cordage Chook
title: Yale Cordage Chook for Synthetic Winch Line
meta: The Yale Cordage Chook is an end fitting for synthetic winch line, sold on its own for re-rigging Ultrex lines. What it is for and how to check it.
tagline: A Yale Cordage end fitting for synthetic winch lines like Ultrex.
summary: The Yale Cordage Chook is the end fitting Yale supplies on its Ultrex synthetic winch lines, sold here on its own. Crews pick it up to re-rig a line, replace a damaged fitting, or set up a line cut from bulk Ultrex.
highlights: End fitting for synthetic winch line
Sold on its own for re-rigging
Handy spare for the winch truck
Confirm size and rating at order time

p: A synthetic winch line is only as good as the hardware on its end. The Chook is the fitting Yale pairs with its Ultrex lines, and buying it separately lets you build your own line from bulk Ultrex or replace a fitting that has been damaged or lost on a job.

Match the fitting to the diameter of line you are running and to the loads your winch can produce, and confirm the rating with the seller before use. You can find bulk Ultrex and finished lines in rigging rope and winch line.

Attach the fitting to the line as the manufacturer specifies; a poorly made connection is the weak point in the whole setup. If you are not sure how to terminate synthetic line, have it done by someone trained in splicing.

Check the fitting before each use for cracks, deformation, sharp edges that could cut the line, and wear where it bears on the rope. Inspect synthetic winch line for cuts, abrasion, melted or fused fibers, and heavy discoloration, and replace it if the line is damaged. Keep everyone out of the line of pull while winching, and use the winch and line only within their rated capacity and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Does the Chook fit every Ultrex diameter?
faq.a: Check the listing for the line sizes it is made for and match it to your winch line.

faq.q: Can I put the Chook on steel cable?
faq.a: It is meant for Yale's synthetic winch lines. Use the hardware specified by your winch and cable makers for steel.

meta: Yale Ultrex 1/2 in synthetic winch line sold by the foot for building winch and pulling lines. Why crews use synthetic and how to inspect it.
tagline: Bulk 1/2 in Ultrex synthetic line, cut to length for your winch or pulling setup.
summary: Yale Ultrex synthetic winch line in 1/2 in is sold by the foot so you can build a winch line or pulling line to the exact length you need. At 1/2 in it is a heavier line for big winches, log skidding, and pulling equipment.
highlights: Light, flexible, and no wire burrs
Terminate with suitable hardware or splices

p: Buying Ultrex by the foot lets you set the exact length your drum holds or your pull requires, instead of settling for a stock length. At 1/2 in it is a heavier line for big winches, log skidding, and pulling equipment. Synthetic line is much lighter than steel, handles easily in gloves, and does not develop broken wire strands.

You will need to terminate the ends with suitable hardware or a splice. If you are not trained in splicing this kind of line, have a rope shop do it. Finished lines and fittings are in rigging rope and winch line.
Match the diameter to the winch maker's specification and use a smooth hawse fairlead where possible. Spool the line under some tension, and keep it off hot exhaust, sharp edges, and rough concrete.

Bulk line is also handy for spares. Keeping extra on the shelf means a damaged winch line can be cut back, re-terminated, and put back to work instead of waiting on a finished replacement. Some crews also cut short lengths for pulling lines and tag lines around equipment, where light weight and low stretch both help.

Inspect synthetic winch line for cuts, abrasion, melted or fused fibers, and heavy discoloration, and replace it if the line is damaged. Keep everyone out of the line of pull while winching, and use the winch and line only within their rated capacity and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: How much line should I order?
faq.a: Measure what your drum holds at the right diameter and allow extra for the splice or termination. Do not overfill the drum.

faq.q: Can I splice Ultrex myself?
faq.a: Many single braid synthetics can be spliced by hand, but get trained on the correct splice for this line, or have a rope shop do it.

name: DMM Tendon
title: DMM Tendon Saddle Accessory
meta: The DMM Tendon is a saddle accessory for arborist climbers. Where it fits in your setup, how to check compatibility, and what to inspect before use.
tagline: A DMM saddle accessory for climbers fine-tuning their harness setup.
summary: The DMM Tendon is a saddle accessory from DMM, the Welsh maker of carabiners and climbing hardware. It is one of the small parts that let climbers set up their saddle the way they work, so check the listing for its exact fit before ordering.
highlights: Small part for customizing your setup
Inspect along with the rest of your harness

p: Saddle accessories are the small parts that make a harness work for the way you climb: keeping gear where you can reach it, connecting components, or replacing worn pieces. The DMM Tendon belongs to this group. Confirm what it attaches to and which saddles it fits before you order, since saddle hardware is not always cross-compatible.
If you are building out or repairing a harness, browse the rest of saddle parts and shoulder harnesses for related pieces.

Only use an accessory for the job its maker intended. A part made for gear storage or organization is not a life-support connection, and nothing should be added to the life-support parts of a saddle unless the saddle maker allows it.

Small saddle parts are easy to overlook until one is missing. When you set up a new harness or replace a worn one, think through where each tool, cord, and piece of hardware will ride, and which small accessories keep that layout tidy. A clean setup means less fumbling aloft and fewer dropped tools. Keep the packaging or product card with the part so you know exactly what it is rated for, and replace it with the same part when it wears out.

Check the part every day along with the rest of your saddle for cuts, abrasion, cracks, and wear, and replace it when in doubt. Life-support gear must meet ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, be inspected before use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Will the DMM Tendon fit my saddle?
faq.a: Check the listing and the saddle maker's information for compatibility before buying.

faq.q: Is it a life-support component?
faq.a: Treat it as rated only for what DMM states. Do not use any accessory for life support unless its maker rates it for that.

name: Husqvarna 4 in Climber's Wedge
title: Husqvarna 4 in Climber's Wedge
meta: Husqvarna 4 in climber's wedge, a small plastic wedge to carry on your saddle for back cuts aloft. How climbers use it and why it beats a big wedge.
tagline: A small 4 in wedge that rides on your saddle for cuts up in the tree.
summary: The Husqvarna climber's wedge is a small 4 in plastic wedge sized to clip to a saddle and use aloft. It keeps a kerf open on a top or leader so the bar does not get pinched while you finish the cut.
highlights: 4 in long, sized for use aloft
Plastic, so it will not ruin a chain
Light enough to carry on a saddle
Keeps the kerf open on back cuts

body.h: Why climbers carry a small wedge
p: A pinched bar halfway up a tree is a bad place to be. A small wedge tapped into the back cut keeps the kerf open and helps tip a top in the direction you planned. Full-size felling wedges are too heavy and long for this, which is why climbers carry a short one like this 4 in Husqvarna wedge.

Because it is plastic, nicking it with the chain will not damage the cutters the way steel would. Clip it to a gear loop with a light tether so it is not dropped on the ground crew. Other parts and accessories are in saddle parts and accessories.

Set the wedge as soon as you have room in the back cut, and tap it with the flat of a hand saw handle or a small mallet rather than the saw. A small wedge helps with lean but cannot overcome a heavy back lean on its own; plan the cut and rigging for the piece you are taking.

Climbers on removals reach for one most often when taking a top with little lean or a slight back lean, or when a leader starts to sit down on the bar partway through the cut. Having the wedge on the saddle means you do not need to send a line down for one. Carry two if you are taking several tops in a day.
Replace a wedge once it is badly chewed, cracked, or mushroomed. Work aloft only with proper training and a tie-in system that meets ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Is a 4 in wedge enough for felling a whole tree?
faq.a: No. It is sized for tops and leaders aloft. Use full-size felling wedges on the ground.

faq.q: How do I carry it?
faq.a: Most climbers hang it on a gear loop or tool clip with a light tether so it cannot fall on the ground crew.

name: Reecoil Audax 1500 Hydration Harness
title: Reecoil Audax 1500 Hydration Harness
meta: The Reecoil Audax 1500 hydration harness keeps water on you while you climb or work the ground. What it is for and how to fit it with your saddle.
tagline: A hydration harness that keeps water on you through a long climb.
summary: The Reecoil Audax 1500 hydration harness lets climbers and ground crew carry water on their body, so you can drink without coming down or walking back to the truck. The 1500 in the name points to a reservoir of about 1.5 liters.
highlights: Hydration harness worn on the body
About 1.5 liter capacity, per the model name
Drink without coming out of the tree
Useful on hot days and long removals

p: On a hot day a long climb can drain you before you realize it, and coming down for a drink costs time. A hydration harness keeps a reservoir on your back with a drinking tube near your mouth, so you can sip between cuts. The Audax 1500 is made for people who work at height and on the ground.

Check how it sits with your saddle, shoulder straps, and chest harness before you climb; nothing should interfere with your life-support connections or your access to gear. See other saddle parts and shoulder harnesses to round out your setup.

Adjust the straps so the pack rides snug without shifting when you move around the tree. Route the drinking tube so it cannot snag on branches or get near a running chain. Empty, rinse, and dry the reservoir after use so it stays clean.

It also cuts down on trips to the cooler for the ground crew, who can wear it while dragging brush or feeding the chipper. Staying hydrated keeps your judgment sharp, which matters when you are making cuts aloft or working around a running chipper.

A hydration harness is not a life-support component. Keep your climbing system as specified by the manufacturer and ANSI Z133, inspect it before each climb, and make sure you are trained for the work.

faq.q: Can I wear it with a chest harness?
faq.a: Usually, but check the fit with your own saddle and chest harness before climbing so nothing interferes with your connections.

faq.q: How much water does it hold?
faq.a: The 1500 model name points to about 1.5 liters. Confirm the reservoir size on the listing.

name: Teufelberger treeMOTION Gear Loop Assembly
title: Teufelberger treeMOTION Gear Loop Assembly
meta: Replacement gear loop assembly for the Teufelberger treeMOTION saddle. Keep tools and hardware organized and swap out a worn loop in the field.
tagline: A replacement gear loop for treeMOTION saddles.
summary: The Teufelberger treeMOTION gear loop assembly replaces a worn or damaged gear loop on a treeMOTION saddle. Gear loops take a beating from carabiners, saws, and branches, and swapping one out is cheaper than retiring a good saddle.
highlights: Replacement gear loop for treeMOTION saddles
Check fit for your saddle version

p: Gear loops hold your carabiners, prusiks, hand saw, and spare hardware where you can reach them. When one gets cut, frayed, or cracked, gear ends up hanging in the wrong place or falling out of the tree. This assembly lets you restore the loop on a treeMOTION without sending the saddle away.
There have been several treeMOTION versions, so confirm the assembly fits yours before ordering. More replacement parts are in saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.

body.h: Gear loops are not tie-in points
p: Gear loops are for storage only. Never clip a lanyard, climbing system, or rigging into one. Load only what the manufacturer allows, and keep heavy items like a saw on a hook or attachment made for that weight.

Fit the new assembly before your next climb rather than making do with a damaged loop. A loop that tears under a load of carabiners can drop gear on the people below. It is a small part, but it decides where your hardware rides all day, so it is worth keeping right. Order a spare if you run more than one treeMOTION on the crew.

Fit the part as Teufelberger instructs, and inspect it with the rest of your saddle before every climb. Life-support gear must meet ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and climbers should be trained.

faq.q: Will this fit every treeMOTION?
faq.a: Check the listing against your saddle version. Teufelberger has updated the treeMOTION over the years.

faq.q: Can I hang my chainsaw on a gear loop?
faq.a: Use a dedicated saw hook or attachment rated for the saw's weight, not a general gear loop.

name: Tree Access Replacement Rope Bridge with Gyro 3 Swivel
title: Replacement Rope Bridge with Gyro 3 Swivel
h1: Tree Access Replacement Rope Bridge with Gyro 3 Swivel
meta: Tree Access replacement rope bridge with a Gyro 3 swivel for arborist saddles. When to replace a bridge, how to check fit, and what to inspect daily.
tagline: A replacement saddle bridge with a swivel to keep your system from twisting.
summary: This Tree Access replacement rope bridge with Gyro 3 swivel lets you replace a worn bridge on your saddle and add a swivel at the same time. The swivel helps keep your climbing system from twisting as you move around the tree.
highlights: Replacement rope bridge for arborist saddles
Reduces twist in your climbing system
Bridges are a wear item; replace early
Check fit and length for your saddle

p: The bridge is where your climbing system connects to the saddle, and it wears faster than almost anything else on the harness. Hardware slides back and forth on it all day. A worn, glazed, or cut bridge must be replaced, and this kit gives you a new bridge with a swivel included.

A swivel on the bridge lets your climbing system rotate as you work around the tree, which cuts down on rope twist. Confirm the bridge length and attachment style match your saddle. More parts are in saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.

Install the bridge exactly as the saddle and bridge makers instruct, with the correct knots or terminations, and have a qualified person check it if you are not sure. Do not mix parts that the saddle maker does not approve.

Many climbers keep a spare bridge with them so a worn one can be swapped before it becomes a problem. Look at the bridge every time you put the saddle on, and pay particular attention to the spots where carabiners or a ring sit most of the time.

Inspect the bridge and swivel before every climb for glazing, cuts, abrasion, and any stiffness or play in the swivel. Life-support gear must meet ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, be inspected before use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: How often should I replace my bridge?
faq.a: Whenever inspection shows glazing, cuts, or wear, and according to the saddle maker's guidance. Many climbers keep a spare.

faq.q: Do I need a swivel on my bridge?
faq.a: It is not required, but it helps manage twist in your system. Make sure it is approved for your saddle.

name: CAMP Kilo Tool Hook
title: CAMP Kilo Tool Hook for Saws and Gear
meta: The CAMP Kilo tool hook hangs a saw, rope bag, or gear on your saddle or a tree. What it holds, where to clip it, and why it is not a life-support connector.
tagline: A large tool hook for hanging saws and gear on your saddle.
summary: The CAMP Kilo tool hook is a large clip for hanging a saw, rope bag, or other gear on your saddle or a branch. It is a tool-holding hook, not a climbing carabiner, so it stays out of your life-support system.
highlights: Large opening for saw handles and bags
Hang gear on a saddle or a limb

p: Climbers need somewhere to put a top-handle saw, a pole saw head, or a rope bag that will not tangle with the rest of their gear. The CAMP Kilo gives you a wide-mouth hook that is easy to clip and unclip in gloves, whether it lives on a saddle attachment point or gets hung over a limb as a temporary gear station.
Its size makes it easier to use than a regular carabiner when you are juggling a running saw. Compare other saddle storage options for different setups.

body.h: Keep it out of your life-support system
p: Tool hooks are made to hold tools. Never use one to connect a climbing line, lanyard, or rigging, and keep it clearly separate from your life-support carabiners so nobody grabs the wrong one in a hurry.

It is also useful on the ground. Hang it on a limb at shoulder height and you have a spot for the saw and rope bag while you set a throw line, out of the dirt and away from foot traffic. A clean, organized setup is a safer setup, both aloft and on the ground. Mark it with tape or paint so crew members do not confuse it with a rated carabiner.

Check the hook for cracks, sharp edges, and a gate or opening that has been bent out of shape. Inspect your climbing gear daily, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and make sure you are trained.

faq.q: Can I hang a chainsaw on the Kilo?
faq.a: It is made for hanging gear such as saws, but check CAMP's rated load for the weight of your saw.

faq.q: Can I use it as a carabiner?
faq.a: No. It is a tool hook and not rated for life support or rigging.

name: Notch Swinger Tool Carrier
title: Notch Swinger Tool Carrier for Saddles
meta: The Notch Swinger tool carrier hangs a hand saw, pole saw, or small tools on your saddle. How climbers use it and how to keep it out of your tie-in.
tagline: A saddle tool carrier that keeps hand tools hanging where you can reach them.
summary: The Notch Swinger tool carrier hangs from your saddle so a hand saw, pole saw, or other tools hang free and stay in reach. It is a storage accessory, so it lives beside, not inside, your climbing system.
highlights: Keeps saws and tools within reach
Swings free so gear hangs clean

p: The more tools you carry aloft, the more they fight for space on your gear loops. A tool carrier like the Swinger gives a tool its own spot so it hangs clean, swings out of the way when you move, and is easy to grab when you need it.
Set it where it will not snag your lanyard or interfere with your climbing system. Other saddle storage options cover saws and heavier gear.
Keep storage gear clearly separate from life-support connections, and never clip a climbing line, lanyard, or rigging into a tool carrier. Do not overload it beyond what Notch states.

A good carrier also saves your gear loops. Hand saws and pole saw heads hung on regular loops tend to swing into your legs and snag on limbs, and the extra weight wears the loops faster. Giving the tool its own carrier keeps the saddle neater and makes every reach for a tool quicker. Move it around until you find the spot where it hangs clear and is still easy to reach.

Inspect it with the rest of your saddle for wear, cracks, and damaged attachment points, and replace it when worn. Follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions for all climbing gear, and climb only with proper training.

faq.q: What tools can the Swinger carry?
faq.a: It is made for hand tools such as saws. Check the listing for what fits and for any weight limit.

faq.q: Where should I mount it?
faq.a: On a saddle attachment point where it hangs clear of your lanyard and climbing system.

name: Shembiner XLS Chainsaw Hook
title: Shembiner XLS Chainsaw Hook for Saddles
meta: The Shembiner XLS chainsaw hook gives a top-handle saw a quick place to hang on your saddle. What it does, how to set it up, and why it is not life support.
tagline: A saddle-mounted hook that gives your saw its own place to hang.
summary: The Shembiner XLS chainsaw hook gives a climbing saw a dedicated place to hang on your saddle, so you can clip it off quickly between cuts. The XLS is the larger version, with room for bigger saw lanyard rings and handles.
highlights: Dedicated hook for a climbing saw
Quick to clip and unclip between cuts
Keeps the saw off your gear loops

body.h: Giving the saw its own spot
p: A top-handle saw is the heaviest thing most climbers carry, and hanging it on a general gear loop is awkward and hard on the loop. A saw hook like the Shembiner gives it a dedicated, easy-to-reach spot, so you can let go of the saw and grab your hand saw or rope without fumbling.
The XLS size suits larger saw lanyard rings and handles. Compare other saddle storage if you need a smaller hook or a different mount.

Mount it where the saw hangs away from your climbing system and lanyard and does not swing into your legs. Always keep the saw on a saw lanyard as well, so a missed clip does not send it to the ground.

Climbers who run a saw most of the day often say a proper saw hook is one of the cheapest upgrades to their setup. It saves time on every cut, keeps the saw from dangling into the climbing system, and takes the strain off the gear loops. Practice clipping and unclipping it at ground level so the motion is automatic before you are holding a running saw aloft.

A saw hook is a storage accessory. Never use it for life support or rigging. Inspect it for cracks and wear, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and use a chainsaw aloft only with training.

faq.q: Do I still need a saw lanyard?
faq.a: Yes. The hook is for parking the saw. A saw lanyard keeps it attached to you if it slips.

faq.q: What does XLS mean here?
faq.a: It is the larger size in the line, with more room for bigger rings and handles.

name: Replacement Microphone for Sena Tufftalk Lite
title: Sena Tufftalk Lite Replacement Microphone
h1: Replacement Microphone for Sena Tufftalk Lite
meta: Replacement microphone for the Sena Tufftalk Lite earmuff headset. Get crew communication back after a mic gets damaged, torn off, or worn out.
tagline: A replacement boom mic to get a Tufftalk Lite headset talking again.
summary: This Sena Tufftalk Lite replacement microphone restores the mic on your earmuff headset after it gets torn, cracked, or worn out. Swapping the mic is far cheaper than replacing the headset.

p: Headset mics live a hard life on a tree crew: they catch on branches, get knocked by helmets coming off, and get crushed in gear bags. When the mic goes, the climber can still hear but cannot be heard, which defeats the point of a communication headset on a job where clear calls matter.
This replacement is made for the Tufftalk Lite, so you can fix it in the field and keep the crew talking. See other crew communication gear for headsets and accessories.

Follow Sena's instructions to connect the mic to the headset, and position it close to your mouth so it picks up your voice over saw noise. Keep it away from the saw and from pinch points when you take the helmet off.

Keep a spare mic in the truck with the charging cables. A broken mic often happens at the start of a big job, and being able to swap it on the spot keeps the climber and ground crew working with the same calls they rely on every day. Store the spare in a small case so it does not get crushed under other gear.
A headset supports clear communication but does not replace agreed hand signals and command-and-response calls. Set those up with the crew before work starts, as ANSI Z133 expects.

faq.q: Will this mic fit other Sena headsets?
faq.a: It is listed for the Tufftalk Lite. Check compatibility with Sena before using it on another model.

faq.q: Is it hard to install?
faq.a: Follow Sena's instructions; mic replacement is generally a simple swap.

name: Retractable Lanyard with Adhesive Backing for Fox 40 Whistle
title: Retractable Lanyard for Fox 40 Whistle
h1: Retractable Lanyard with Adhesive Backing for Fox 40 Whistle
meta: A retractable lanyard with adhesive backing that keeps a Fox 40 whistle on your helmet or gear. Why crews carry whistles and how to mount the reel.
tagline: A small retractable reel that keeps a whistle where you can reach it.
summary: This retractable whistle lanyard sticks to a helmet, radio, or gear with its adhesive backing and keeps a Fox 40 whistle within reach. Pull the whistle to your mouth, blow, and let it reel back out of the way.
highlights: Retractable cord keeps the whistle tidy
Adhesive backing for helmets and gear

body.h: Why a whistle belongs on every crew
p: Saws and chippers drown out voices, and a whistle cuts through noise when someone needs to stop work or get attention fast. Many crews agree on simple whistle signals, and a whistle only helps if it is on you. This retractable reel keeps it close without a cord dangling around your neck near a running saw.
Stick it on a helmet, radio, or harness strap where you can reach it with either hand. See other crew communication gear for headsets.

Clean and dry the surface before applying the adhesive, press firmly, and let it set before use. Check with the helmet maker before sticking anything to a helmet shell, since some do not allow adhesives.

A whistle is also useful when a radio or headset fails, when a member of the public walks under the work zone, or when someone needs help and cannot get to a radio. The reel keeps the whistle off the ground and out of the gear bag, so it is there the moment you need it. Consider one for every crew member, not only the climber.
Agree on whistle and hand signals with the crew before work starts, and use command-and-response communication as ANSI Z133 expects. A whistle backs up those systems; it does not replace them.

faq.q: Does it come with a whistle?
faq.a: The listing is for the retractable lanyard. Check whether a whistle is included before ordering.

faq.q: Can I stick it on my helmet?
faq.a: Check your helmet maker's guidance first. Some do not allow adhesives or stickers on the shell.

name: Sena Tufftalk Lite Helmet-Mounted Earmuffs
title: Sena Tufftalk Lite Helmet-Mounted Earmuffs
meta: Sena Tufftalk Lite helmet-mounted earmuffs combine hearing protection with Bluetooth crew intercom. What it does on a tree crew and how to fit it.
tagline: Helmet-mount earmuffs with Bluetooth intercom for climber-to-ground talk.
summary: Sena Tufftalk Lite helmet-mounted earmuffs combine hearing protection with Bluetooth intercom, so a climber and ground crew can talk over saw and chipper noise. The helmet-mount version attaches to compatible helmets instead of using a headband.
highlights: Talk over saw and chipper noise

p: Shouting between a climber and the ground crew over a running saw does not work, and missed calls are how pieces get dropped on people. The Tufftalk Lite builds intercom into earmuffs you already need for hearing protection, so climber and groundie can call cuts, lowers, and stops clearly.

The helmet-mount version clips to compatible helmet slots, which keeps it in place on the climb. Check helmet compatibility before ordering. See more crew communication gear, including replacement parts.

Earmuffs only protect your hearing when they seal well, so set the mount for a firm, even seal and check the noise reduction rating on the listing. Charge the headset before each day, and pair units at the truck before anyone climbs.

Headsets also help on the ground. The person on the lowering line can hear the climber's call over the chipper, and the climber can hear when someone is clear of the drop zone. That clearer back and forth speeds up rigging and makes it easier to stop work fast when something looks wrong. Agree on short, standard calls so every message is quick and clear.
Radios and headsets can fail, so keep agreed hand and whistle signals as a backup and use command-and-response communication as ANSI Z133 expects.

faq.q: Will it fit my helmet?
faq.a: It mounts to helmets with compatible accessory slots. Check the listing and your helmet maker's guidance.

faq.q: Can I replace the microphone?
faq.a: Yes. A replacement microphone for the Tufftalk Lite is sold separately.

name: 3M Mesh Screen for Hard Hat (Fits Peltor Muffs)
title: 3M Mesh Screen for Hard Hat, Fits Peltor Muffs
h1: 3M Mesh Screen for Hard Hat, Fits Peltor Muffs
meta: A 3M mesh screen visor for hard hats that pairs with Peltor earmuffs. Keeps chips and sawdust out of your face while you buck and limb on the ground.
tagline: A mesh face screen for hard hats that works with Peltor earmuffs.
summary: This 3M mesh screen mounts on a hard hat alongside Peltor earmuffs to keep chips, sawdust, and twigs off your face while you cut. Mesh stays cooler and fogs less than a clear shield, which is why so many saw users prefer it.
highlights: Mesh face screen for hard hats
Does not fog like a clear shield

p: When you are bucking, limbing, or feeding a chipper, the face takes a steady shower of chips and sawdust. A mesh screen blocks the larger debris while letting air through, so it does not fog up on a hot day or in the rain the way clear plastic does.
This screen mounts with Peltor earmuffs on a hard hat, so you get face and hearing protection together. Check fit with your hard hat and muffs before ordering. Compare other eye protection options.

body.h: It does not replace safety glasses
p: Mesh screens stop chips, not fine dust or small fast fragments. Wear rated safety glasses under the screen every time you run a saw or chipper. Check the screen for tears, dents, and a loose mount, and replace it once damaged.

Mesh screens also make it easier to work in the rain or on cold mornings, when a clear shield fogs from your breath within minutes. Flip it up between cuts to talk with the crew or check a rigging point, then drop it again before you start the saw. Keep a spare screen in the truck in case one is bent.
Follow ANSI Z133 for personal protective equipment on tree work, including eye, face, and hearing protection.

faq.q: Do I still need safety glasses with a mesh screen?
faq.a: Yes. A mesh screen is face protection from larger debris. Wear safety glasses underneath.

faq.q: Will it fit my helmet?
faq.a: It is made to work with Peltor earmuff mounts on hard hats. Check compatibility with your helmet and muffs.

name: 3M SecureFit Protective Eyewear, Clear Lens
title: 3M SecureFit Protective Eyewear, Clear Lens
meta: 3M SecureFit protective eyewear with a clear lens, a light, snug safety glass for climbing, chipping, and saw work. Fit, lens choice, and care tips.
tagline: Light, snug clear safety glasses for everyday tree work.
summary: 3M SecureFit protective eyewear with a clear lens is a lightweight safety glass that stays put under a helmet and earmuffs. Clear lenses suit shaded canopies, overcast days, and early starts.
highlights: Clear lens for low light and shade

body.h: Why clear lenses on a tree crew
p: Eye protection is required for chainsaw work, chipping, and climbing, and the glasses that get worn are the ones that are comfortable. SecureFit is a light, close-fitting style that stays on when you look up into a canopy and does not fight with earmuff cups.
Clear lenses keep you seeing detail in shade, under a dense crown, and on overcast days, where tinted lenses make it hard to read wood and cuts. Compare other eye protection including tinted options.

body.h: Check the rating and keep spares
p: Confirm the eyewear is marked to the impact standard your work requires before you rely on it. Replace glasses with scratched, pitted, or cracked lenses, since damaged lenses hurt vision and protection.

Glasses that sit loose or press on the ears tend to come off, so comfort is really about compliance. Try a pair on with your helmet and earmuffs before buying for the whole crew, and buy in quantity once you find a fit people will wear all day. Keep a lens wipe in your pocket too, since sap and sawdust build up quickly.
Keep a few spare pairs in the truck so nobody works without them. Follow ANSI Z133 for personal protective equipment, and pair glasses with a face screen when chipping or running a saw.

faq.q: Clear or tinted lenses?
faq.a: Clear for shade, overcast days, and canopy work; tinted for bright, open ground work.

faq.q: Will they fit under earmuffs?
faq.a: The thin temples are made to sit comfortably under muffs, though fit varies by person.

name: ERB Safety Clear Safety Glasses
title: ERB Safety Clear Safety Glasses
meta: ERB Safety clear safety glasses, low-cost eye protection for climbing, chipping, and saw work. When to pick clear lenses and how to keep spares on hand.
tagline: Low-cost clear safety glasses to keep a crew in eye protection.
summary: ERB Safety clear safety glasses are an inexpensive way to keep every crew member in eye protection. Clear lenses are the everyday choice for shade, canopy work, overcast days, and early starts.
highlights: Low cost, easy to keep spares

p: Clear lenses are the everyday choice for shade, canopy work, overcast days, and early starts. Pick the lens for the light you work in; tinted lenses in deep shade make it hard to see cuts, and clear lenses in full sun cause squinting.
Because they cost so little, it is easy to stock a box in the truck so nobody has an excuse to work without them. Compare other eye protection if you need a different fit.

body.h: Check the rating and replace often
p: Confirm the glasses are marked to the impact standard your work requires. Replace them once lenses are scratched, pitted, or cracked, since damaged lenses reduce both vision and protection.

Keep both clear and tinted pairs on hand so crew members can match the lens to the light as it changes through the day. Cheap glasses also reduce the temptation to keep wearing a scratched pair. Store them in a case or a clean bag rather than loose on the dash, where they scratch and pick up sap. A scratched lens is cheap to replace, so replace it.
Wear safety glasses for saw work, chipping, and climbing, and add a face screen for heavy chip and sawdust exposure. Follow ANSI Z133 for personal protective equipment.

faq.q: Can I wear these under a mesh face screen?
faq.a: Yes. Safety glasses under a mesh screen is a common setup for saw and chipper work.

faq.q: When should I use clear lenses?
faq.a: Clear lenses are the everyday choice for shade, canopy work, overcast days, and early starts.
